vignette:
Carlos is twenty-four years old, though he looks both younger and older at the same time. He sits at the edge of the armchair in my office, spine straight, hands folded in his lap. He is a financial analyst at a mid-sized firm in the city, and he tells me he is good at his job. He arrives early every morning, leaves late every night, and his spreadsheets are immaculate. He says this without pride. It is simply a fact, like the weather.

He was seventeen when he enlisted. He tells me he joined the Army because his father had served, and because the recruiter came to his high school in the small border town where he grew up. He wanted to see the world, he says, or at least a world bigger than the one he knew. He deployed to Afghanistan at nineteen.

The event that broke him happened during a routine patrol in a village he cannot name. He was the driver of a MRAP. The vehicle ahead of them hit an IED. He remembers the sound first—a pressure that was not just noise but a physical force that pushed into his chest and made his ears ring for days afterward. He remembers stopping, the heat, the dust, the shouting over the radio. He remembers being told to stay in the vehicle, to maintain security. He remembers the shape of the gunner above him, slumped. He remembers the smell—cordite and something else, something sweet and metallic that he still smells in his apartment sometimes, when it is quiet.

He was not physically injured. This is a fact he repeats to me, as if it absolves him of something. He was not hurt. He did what he was told. He stayed in the vehicle.

For the next several months, he finished his deployment. He did his job. He came home. He received a commendation. He used his GI Bill to finish college in three years, double-majoring in finance and economics. He got the job at the firm. He moved into a studio apartment with a view of a parking lot. He bought a couch. He bought a coffee table. He did everything right.

But he cannot sleep. He tells me he averages about three hours a night. He lies in bed and listens to the building settle, to the hum of the refrigerator, to the distant sirens. When he does sleep, he dreams of dust and heat and the shape of the gunner. He wakes up with his heart pounding, his sheets soaked, his hands already reaching for something he no longer carries.

At work, he is precise. He tells me this is the only place he feels in control. The numbers do not lie. They do not surprise him. He can predict the market trends, the quarterly reports, the risk assessments. But sometimes, in the middle of a meeting, a colleague will drop a binder on the table, and Carlos will flinch so hard he nearly knocks his chair over. He will say he is fine. He will excuse himself to the bathroom, where he will stand over the sink and breathe until his hands stop shaking.

He does not date. He tried, once, a few months ago. A woman from the marketing department asked him for coffee. He said yes. They sat at a café, and she asked him about his weekend, and he could not answer. He could not form a sentence that was not about the dust and the heat and the shape of the gunner. He excused himself and walked home. He has not spoken to her since.

He has not told his family. His mother calls every Sunday, and he tells her he is fine, that work is good, that he is eating well. He is not eating well. He has lost fifteen pounds. He tells me he forgets to eat, or that food has no taste, or that he feels nauseous most of the time. He drinks coffee to stay awake and whiskey to fall asleep, and neither works very well.

He came to see me because his boss told him he seemed "off." He came because he is afraid he will lose the only thing that still makes sense—the numbers, the spreadsheets, the clean lines of a quarterly projection. He sits in my office and does not cry. He tells me these things in a flat, careful voice, like he is reading a report. He is very good at his job.
